title: Subject Choice and Career Planning
summary: Choosing subjects for Grades 10 to 12, compulsory and elective subjects, Mathematics or Mathematical Literacy, NSC pass requirements, study pathways, funding, and making a career plan.

notes.text: At the end of Grade 9 you choose the subjects you will take in Grades 10, 11 and 12 (the Further Education and Training, or **FET**, phase). These choices affect what you can study after school, so choose carefully.

rows: e.g. Physical Sciences, Life Sciences, Geography, History
Engineering Graphics and Design, Information Technology, CAT
Tourism, Consumer Studies, Agricultural Sciences, Visual Arts, Music, Dramatic Arts and others

notes.text: **Mathematics** is required for most degrees in engineering, medicine, the natural sciences, actuarial science, accounting and IT. **Mathematical Literacy** focuses on using maths in everyday life (budgets, measurement, maps) and is accepted for many other courses. Choosing Mathematical Literacy may close some doors, so check the requirements of careers you are interested in.

rows: Home Language 40%; 4 subjects from the designated list at 50% or more; 2 further subjects at 30%
Diploma studies at a university of technology or college
Home Language 40%; 4 subjects at 40% or more; 2 further subjects at 30%
Home Language 40%; 2 subjects at 40%; 4 further subjects at 30%

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Universities also set their own entry requirements, usually using an **Admission Point Score (APS)** calculated from your marks, plus minimum marks in specific subjects. Always check the requirements early.

items: The **requirements** of careers you are considering.
Advice from teachers, counsellors and family, but the choice must be **yours**.
Do **not** choose a subject just because your friends are taking it or because it seems easy.
**NSFAS** (National Student Financial Aid Scheme): bursaries for students from households with a low income, at public universities and TVET colleges.
Bursaries from companies, government departments and SETAs, often linked to working for the sponsor afterwards.
Merit scholarships for excellent marks, and study loans from banks.
Know yourself: interests, abilities, values and personality.
Research careers: duties, qualifications, demand and salary.
Choose subjects that keep your options open.
Set short-, medium- and long-term goals.
Find out about institutions, applications and funding.
Gain experience: job shadowing, volunteering, holiday work.

questions.prompt: Name TWO ways to fund studies after school.
